newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan premium widens as Tokyo stocks fall.
newsitem.headline: Japan premium widens as Tokyo stocks fall.

text.p: The Japan premium -- the extra cost Japanese banks are charged when raising funds in the Euro interbank market -- rose on Tuesday as the recent downtrend in Tokyo stocks fuelled concerns over Japan's financial system.
Major Japanese banks were paying a premium of about 15 basis points over the prevailing three-month Eurodollar deposit rate of 5.59375 percent, money traders said.

This compared with a premium of about six basis points early last week. The Japan premium started to pick up on Friday after the key Nikkei stock average lost more then 2,000 points during its first week of trading in 1997 and fell below the key 18,000 level, they said.
The Nikkei average of 225 leading shares closed down 25.66 points or 0.14 percent at 18,093.13 on Tuesday after a rebound on Monday from last week's falls.

"Lower share prices weaken banks' financial conditions. Thus, when the stock market falls, the Japan premium is inclined to rise," said a money trader, adding that a fall below 17,000 in the Nikkei average might cause a further rise in the Japan premium.
Equity portfolios account for a significant percentage of Japanese banks' risk-weighted capital.
Japanese banks paid a premium of as high as 40 basis points in late December, when foreign banks were reluctant to lend money ahead of year-end book closings.

The premium for major Japanese city banks was close to zero until debt-laden Hanwa Bank Ltd, a regional bank in western Japan, was ordered to halt operations by regulators in late November, traders said.
